sections.content: You know *haber* from the present perfect (A2 Unit 1): *he*, *has*, *ha*, *hemos*, *han*. The same forms, followed by *de* and an infinitive, make a formal pattern that you mostly read in books, speeches and careful writing. It has two uses. The first is a duty, a little more serious than *tener que*: *He de reconocer que tienes razón* is "I must admit that you are right". The second is for stories: *había de* or *habría de* + infinitive says what was going to happen later, as if the writer already knew: *Aquel viaje había de cambiar su vida* is "That journey was to change his life".
sections.title: A formal pattern
haber de + infinitive
rows: He de reconocer que tienes razón.
I must admit that you are right.
Los estudiantes han de llegar antes de las nueve.
Students are to arrive before nine.
Aquel viaje había de cambiar su vida.
That journey was to change his life.
Años después, aquella casa habría de convertirse en un museo.
Years later, that house was to become a museum.

sections.content: Do not confuse *haber de* with *hay que*. *Haber de* changes with the person (*he de*, *has de*, *hemos de*), but *hay que* never does. In everyday speech people say *tengo que* or *debo* instead, so use *haber de* when you want to sound formal or when you tell a story.
